title: Loans as Cold War reward and punishment
summary:
US officials used their votes and influence at the IMF, World Bank, Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and the US Export-Import Bank to cut credit to governments they opposed and to open it to governments they backed. The clearest record is Chile. The US Senate Church Committee (1975) found that after Salvador Allende's election in 1970, Washington halted new bilateral aid (NSDM 93, November 1970), Export-Import Bank credits fell to zero in 1971, IDB loans fell from $46 million in 1970 to $2 million in 1972, the World Bank made no new loans from 1970 to 1973, and US short-term commercial credit fell from about $300 million under Frei to about $30 million in 1972. CIA Director Richard Helms's notes of his 15 September 1970 meeting with President Nixon read "Make the economy scream." Military aid to Chile was not cut, and US military sales rose sharply from 1973 to 1974, after the September 1973 coup.

The same pattern runs through other declassified US records. In Brazil, after the April 1964 coup, the US gave a $50 million AID loan in June 1964, a $150 million program loan in December 1964, and backed a $125 million IMF standby in 1965 (FRUS). In Indonesia, after Suharto displaced Sukarno, the State Department set up a multilateral 'Aid to Indonesia Club' with Japan, the IMF and World Bank (1966), creditors rescheduled over $300 million of arrears (December 1966) and the US committed to one-third of the aid total to back the leaders of Indonesia's anti-Communist turn (FRUS). Allies such as Mobutu's Zaire and Marcos's Philippines kept receiving loans despite known corruption; opponents such as Sandinista Nicaragua saw US 'no' votes at the IDB and World Bank. After the Cold War, debt relief and loans flowed to front-line allies: Egypt after the 1991 Gulf War and Pakistan after September 2001. Peer-reviewed studies support a link but with limits: Thacker (1999, 87 countries, 1985-94) found that moving toward the US in UN votes raised the odds of an IMF loan; Dreher and Jensen (2007, 206 IMF letters of intent, 38 countries, 1997-2003) found close US allies got loans with fewer conditions.

countries.note: The White House, NSC, CIA, Treasury and State Department set lending policy toward Chile (NSDM 93, 1970), Brazil (AID program loans, 1964-66) and Indonesia (one-third aid share, 1966-69), according to the Church Committee report and FRUS documents. The US is the IMF's largest shareholder, which Thacker (1999) and Dreher and Jensen (2007) use to explain their statistical findings.

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: Under Allende (1970-73), Ex-Im credits fell from $234 million (1967) to zero (1971), IDB loans fell from $46 million (1970) to $2 million (1972) and the World Bank made no new loans, per the Church Committee. The IMF still extended about $90 million in 1971-72. Military aid continued, and military sales rose sharply from 1973 to 1974 after the coup (Church Committee). In November 1986 the US abstained, after telling Congress it would vote no, on a World Bank loan to Pinochet's Chile (Christian Science Monitor, 1987).

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: After the April 1964 coup against Goulart, the US gave a $50 million AID contingency loan (June 1964), a $150 million program loan (December 1964), a $53.6 million Treasury exchange agreement, and the IMF agreed a $125 million standby (1965). In December 1965 Rusk asked Johnson for another $150 million, saying political factors strongly supported it; Johnson approved it and it was signed in February 1966 (FRUS 1964-68 vol. XXXI, doc. 224).

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: Under Somoza, Nicaragua received nine World Bank loans in 1951-56 and one in 1960, per the Bank's official history as quoted by Toussaint, and the Bank's board approved another on 12 April 1961. Under the Sandinistas, the US cast the only 'no' vote on a $16 million World Bank loan (January 1982), vetoed a $2.2 million IDB road loan that 42 other members approved (June 1983), and Nicaragua got no IDB loans in 1984 (Multinational Monitor, 1985). A 1988 Heritage Foundation paper says the IDB approved no new loans to Nicaragua after 1983 under US State Department pressure.

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: The World Bank sent a survey mission in 1951 but made no loan until 1955, after the CIA-backed overthrow of President Arbenz in 1954, according to Toussaint citing the Bank's official history (Kapur, Lewis and Webb, 1997, vol. 1, p. 103).

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: Michael Manley's government broke off talks with the IMF in March 1980 over a $175 million credit and its budget conditions (Christian Science Monitor, 1980). After Edward Seaga took office in late 1980, the IMF agreed a package of about $650-700 million over three years (April 1981), with $60 million from the US government and a US business committee chaired by David Rockefeller (Christian Science Monitor 1981; Multinational Monitor 1981).

In August 1966 Rusk told Johnson that an informal 'Aid to Indonesia Club' had met in Tokyo and that the IMF and World Bank must play a key role in rebuilding Indonesia's economy (FRUS doc. 215). Creditors rescheduled over $300 million in arrears (December 1966); donors pledged about $200 million for 1967, the US committing one-third ($65 million). In April 1969 the US pledged about $123 million, one-third of a $365 million non-food aid request (FRUS docs. 241 and 1969-76 vol. XX doc. 267).

In June 1981 the IMF approved a three-year loan of about $1.1-1.2 billion to Mobutu's Zaire, and in July 12 Western governments rescheduled about $600 million (Multinational Monitor 1981; Christian Science Monitor 1983). US Treasury official Alexis Rieffel said withdrawing support from Mobutu would cause 'a breakdown of law and order'. A report for the IMF by Erwin Blumenthal, leaked in 1982, said creditors had no chance of repayment because of corruption (Christian Science Monitor, 1982).

The Philippines kept borrowing after Marcos declared martial law in 1972: external debt rose from $2.3 billion (1970) to over $17.2 billion (1980), per the US Library of Congress country study. Toussaint's figures on World Bank lending to Marcos are listed under one author's claims.

After Mubarak joined the US-led Gulf War coalition, the US forgave $7.1 billion of military debt (December 1990), Gulf states forgave about $7 billion, and on 25 May 1991 Paris Club creditors agreed to write off 50% of $20.2 billion in phases; the IMF approved a $372 million standby (Christian Science Monitor, May and July 1991).

After September 2001, the IMF approved a $1.32 billion three-year loan (announced 7 December 2001) and the Paris Club restructured about $12.5 billion of debt (13 December 2001). Dawn (2002) reported $1.5 billion in aid offered in four months, including a $673 million US grant within a $1 billion package; a World Bank official in Islamabad said the support was based on reforms, not politics.

timeline.event: The World Bank makes its first loan to Guatemala, a year after the 1954 overthrow of President Arbenz; a survey mission in 1951 had led to no loan.
On 12 April the World Bank board approves a loan to Somoza's Nicaragua, days before the Bay of Pigs invasion, which Toussaint says was launched from Nicaraguan territory.
After the April coup in Brazil, the US gives a $50 million AID contingency loan in June and a $150 million program loan in December.
Brazil's military government gets a $125 million IMF standby and a $53.6 million US Treasury exchange agreement; in December Rusk asks Johnson for another $150 million, citing political factors.
In August Rusk tells Johnson that an informal 'Aid to Indonesia Club' has met in Tokyo and that the IMF and World Bank must play a key role in Indonesia's recovery.
A State Department paper records creditors rescheduling over $300 million of Indonesian arrears (December 1966), $200 million pledged for 1967, and a US commitment of one-third.
Rogers asks Nixon to confirm a US pledge of one-third (about $123 million) of Indonesia's $365 million non-food aid request at the IGGI meeting of 14 April.
Helms's notes of his 15 September meeting with Nixon on Chile read 'Make the economy scream'; NSDM 93 in November halts new bilateral aid.
US Export-Import Bank credits to Chile fall to zero, and a $21 million credit for Boeing jets is deferred in August.
Nixon says in January the US will withhold support from loans under consideration in multilateral banks; IDB loans to Chile fall to $2 million.
US military sales to Chile rise sharply from 1973 to 1974, after the coup that brought Pinochet to power.
Jamaica's Manley government breaks off IMF talks on a $175 million credit over budget conditions.
Under Seaga, Jamaica agrees an IMF package of close to $700 million over three years, with more from other lenders and banks.
The IMF approves a $1.1 billion three-year loan to Zaire; a US Treasury official cites the risk of disorder if support for Mobutu is withdrawn.
In June the US vetoes a $2.2 million IDB road loan to Nicaragua that the other 42 members approved.
In November the US abstains, after saying it would vote no, on a World Bank loan to Pinochet's Chile.
In December the US forgives $7.1 billion of Egypt's military debt after Egypt joins the Gulf War coalition.
On 25 May Paris Club creditors agree to write off 50% of $20.2 billion owed by Egypt; the IMF approves a $372 million standby.
In early December the IMF approves a $1.32 billion three-year loan to Pakistan, and on 13 December the Paris Club restructures about $12.5 billion of its debt.

claims_per_author.author: Michael Moffitt and Isabel Letelier
claims_per_author.work: 'Private International Banks Support Chilean Junta', Multinational Monitor, Winter 1978-79
claims_per_author.claim: Moffitt and Letelier say the junta received nearly $350 million in US aid after 1973, including $125 million committed in 1974, about $400 million from multilateral banks and $380 million from the IMF, against under $25 million in US aid to Allende over three years.
claims_per_author.status: The Church Committee confirms the credit cut under Allende and a sharp rise in US military sales after the coup, but gives no clear post-coup economic aid total. The article names no source for its aid totals, and its private bank figures come from a 'confidential source'.

claims_per_author.author: Eric Toussaint (CADTM)
claims_per_author.work: 'Bolsonaro has announced a celebration of the 1964 military coup', Against the Current No. 200, May/June 2019
claims_per_author.claim: Toussaint says World Bank and IMF loans to Brazil had been suspended for three years before the 1964 coup and resumed very soon after it.
claims_per_author.status: FRUS doc. 224 confirms large US loans and an IMF standby after the coup; the pre-coup suspension is not confirmed in the US records checked, and Toussaint does not say why lending stopped.

claims_per_author.author: Eric Toussaint (CADTM)
claims_per_author.work: 'The World Bank and the Philippines', International Viewpoint
claims_per_author.claim: Toussaint says World Bank lending to Marcos rose from $30 million to $165 million in 1974 and reached $600 million in 1983, and, quoting the Bank's official history, that McNamara and Bank staff welcomed Marcos's rule by decree.
claims_per_author.status: He cites Kapur, Lewis and Webb, The World Bank: Its First Half Century (1997), vol. 1, pp. 303-304, 558 and 563, which was not checked directly. His footnote for the 1974 figures does not support them, and the 1972 memo he quotes speaks of lending 50% more, not double.

claims_per_author.author: Multinational Monitor (unsigned)
claims_per_author.work: 'Taking Care of Business in Nicaragua', April 1985
claims_per_author.claim: The article lists each US vote against or veto of IDB and World Bank loans to Sandinista Nicaragua in 1981-85.
claims_per_author.status: A Heritage Foundation paper (1988) separately says the IDB approved no new loans to Nicaragua after 1983 under US State Department pressure. The individual votes were not checked against IDB or World Bank board records. Toussaint, citing the Bank's history, says the World Bank suspended lending over arrears.

claims_per_author.author: Eric Toussaint (CADTM)
claims_per_author.work: 'A Brief History of the Relations between the World Bank, the IMF, the US Government and Nicaragua', International Viewpoint, 2018
claims_per_author.claim: Toussaint says the World Bank did not resume lending to Nicaragua until the Sandinistas lost the February 1990 election to the US-backed Violeta Chamorro.
claims_per_author.status: Not checked against World Bank project records.

uncertain: How much of the World Bank's halt to Chile in 1970-73 came from US pressure and how much from the Bank's own view of Chile's creditworthiness and expropriations is disputed; the Church Committee says the US effort to enlist the banks was only partly successful.
Kedar (2018) finds the World Bank used its claim of economic neutrality to resist US attempts to tie loans to Pinochet to human rights in 1973-77, so the Bank was not always a tool of Washington.

The statistical evidence is limited: Thacker (1999) found that a country's level of alignment with the US did not predict IMF loans in 1985-89, only movement toward the US did; alignment level also mattered in 1990-94.
Dreher and Jensen's finding that close US allies get fewer IMF conditions covers 1997-2003 only and does not show the US directly instructed IMF staff.
For Pakistan in 2001, a World Bank office and an official denied that the US or G-8 pressed the lenders to help because of Musharraf's support for the war in Afghanistan.
The post-coup Chile aid totals rest on one magazine account, and the individual US votes on Nicaragua loans rest on another; both need checking against IDB and World Bank board records.
Brazil's treatment before the 1964 coup (whether lending was deliberately withheld from Goulart) is not documented in the records consulted.

Dreher and Sturm (2012, 188 countries, 1970-2008) found that World Bank adjustment loans and large non-concessional loans go with more voting alongside the G7 at the UN, but IMF loans did not show this link to voting with the US.
check_note: The 1978 magazine figures on US aid to Pinochet ($350 million, $125 million in 1974) were taken out of the summary, the Chile note, the links and the timeline and left only as the authors' claim, because the article names no source; they were replaced with the Church Committee finding that military sales rose sharply after the coup. Toussaint's World Bank lending figures for the Philippines and his Brazil and Nicaragua 1990 points were moved to one author's claims; his footnote does not support the 1974 figures. The Indonesia quote 'anti-Communist leadership' is not in the FRUS document and was reworded. Somoza-era loans were corrected to nine in 1951-56 plus one in 1960, with a further loan in April 1961. The IMF date for Pakistan was softened because the Paris Club gives 6 December and the IMF release 7 December. A Heritage Foundation paper was added as a second account of the US block on IDB loans to Nicaragua, and the Thacker caveat was narrowed to 1985-89.

title: Debts run up by dictators, paid by those after them
summary:
Banks, governments and international lenders lent to dictators who wasted or stole much of the money, and the governments that followed were made to pay it back. In Argentina, external debt rose from $7.5 billion to $43.5 billion under the 1976-1983 junta, according to Jubilee 2000; on 13 July 2000 federal judge Jorge Ballestero, ruling on a complaint filed by Alejandro Olmos in 1982, found 477 illegal acts and said the link between the debt and its costs could not have gone unnoticed by the IMF officials supervising the talks. The crimes were time-barred, so the ruling went to Congress, which created a standing debt monitoring commission in 2014. In the Philippines, the Marcos government borrowed from the US Export-Import Bank to build the $2.3 billion Bataan nuclear plant with Westinghouse; it never produced electricity, and the public finished paying P64.7 billion (P43.5 billion principal, P21.2 billion interest) in April 2007. A Philippine anti-graft court in 2012 ruled that the $50.6 million commission paid to Marcos associate Herminio Disini was ill-gotten.

Peer-reviewed work links such loans to capital flight. Ndikumana and Boyce (1998) found Mobutu's Zaire ran up about $14 billion in public external debt while capital flight reached $12 billion by 1990; their 2008 study of 40 sub-Saharan countries (1970-2004) estimated that up to 62 cents of each dollar borrowed abroad left the region as capital flight, most of it in the same year. In 2004 the Paris Club wrote off 80% of Iraq's $38.9 billion debt from the Saddam era, and the US forgave its full $4.1 billion, and the relief went through the usual Paris Club process tied to an IMF programme, not an odious-debt ruling. Ecuador's 2007-2008 audit commission called much of its debt illegitimate; Ecuador stopped paying $3.2 billion of bonds and in 2009 bought about 91% of them back at 35 cents on the dollar. On 2 October 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 520 million owed by five countries from its 1976-80 ship export campaign, saying it shared responsibility for a development policy failure.

countries.note: External debt rose from $7.5 billion to $43.5 billion under the 1976-83 junta, according to Jubilee 2000. Judge Ballestero's 13 July 2000 ruling in the Olmos case found 477 illegal acts; because they were time-barred, he sent the matter to Congress, which created a standing debt monitoring commission in 2014 (Law 26.984). The Jubilee 2000 account named Barclays and Lloyds among about 30 British lenders of the period.

An audit commission set up by decree in July 2007 reviewed debts from 1976 to 2007 and in November 2008 called much of the debt illegitimate, accusing Salomon Smith Barney of handling the 2000 restructuring without Ecuador's authorization. Ecuador stopped paying $3.2 billion of 2012 and 2030 bonds and in 2009 repurchased about 91% at 35 cents on the dollar, spending about $900 million. In 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 225 million of Ecuador's ship export debt.

External debt rose from $2.3 billion in 1970 to over $17.2 billion in 1980 (Library of Congress country study). The Bataan plant, financed by the US Export-Import Bank, cost $2.3 billion, never produced electricity, and was fully paid off in April 2007 at P64.7 billion. The Philippines lost its bribery case against Westinghouse in a US court in 1993 and signed a $100 million settlement with the company in October 1995.

Under Mobutu, public external debt reached about $14 billion and capital flight about $12 billion by 1990, nearly $18 billion with interest (Ndikumana and Boyce, 1998). A report for the IMF by Erwin Blumenthal, leaked in 1982, said creditors had no chance of repayment because of corruption.

Jubilee 2000's South African branch put the apartheid-era debt at R86.7 billion in 1993 (about $14 billion at 1999 rates); the post-apartheid government did not seek cancellation. Over a fifth of the 1999 budget went to debt service, but more than 95% of that debt was owed inside South Africa (The Economist via Probe International). A 1999 Jubilee report named German, Swiss, British, US and French banks as creditors (Cape Times).

Foreign debt was $750 million when Jean-Claude Duvalier fled in 1986, according to Toussaint and Perchellet (CADTM), and more than half of Haiti's debt was contracted under the Duvaliers (1957-86), according to a Foreign Policy In Focus article. About $1.2 billion was cancelled under the HIPC initiative in 2009. Duvalier assets remained frozen at UBS in Switzerland in 2010 (CADTM).

Iraq's public debt was about $120 billion at end-2004. On 21 November 2004 the Paris Club agreed to cut 80% of the $38.9 billion owed to it in three phases tied to an IMF programme, and the US forgave its $4.1 billion on 17 December 2004 (CRS report RS21765).
On 2 October 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 168 million owed by Egypt from the 1976-80 ship export campaign.
In 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 19 million owed by Jamaica from the ship export campaign.
In 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 48 million owed by Peru from the ship export campaign.
In 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 60 million owed by Sierra Leone from the ship export campaign; only this part was to be paid for from Norway's debt relief facility.

On 2 October 2006 Norway announced it would cancel NOK 520 million owed by five countries, calling its 1976-80 ship export campaign a development policy failure for which it shared responsibility. It did not count the cancellation as aid.

The US Export-Import Bank financed the Bataan plant built by Pittsburgh-based Westinghouse. The US forgave all $4.1 billion of Iraq's debt to it in December 2004 at a cost of $360 million to the Treasury (CRS).

On 13 May Jeffrey Winters tells the US Senate that a third of World Bank loan funds to Indonesia were stolen.
On 21 November the Paris Club agrees to cut 80% of Iraq's $38.9 billion debt; on 17 December the US forgives its $4.1 billion.

Ecuador buys back about 91% of its defaulted 2012 and 2030 bonds at 35 cents on the dollar.
On 11 April the Sandiganbayan rules the $50.6 million Bataan commission paid to Herminio Disini ill-gotten.

claims_per_author.author: Jeffrey Winters
claims_per_author.work: Testimony to the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 13 May 2004
claims_per_author.claim: Winters says a third of World Bank loan funds to Indonesia under Suharto were stolen, and that the Bank took part 'mostly passively' in the corruption of roughly $100 billion of its loans worldwide.
claims_per_author.status: Winters says the World Bank publicly denied his 1997 allegation and called him irresponsible, and that two leaked internal Bank documents later supported him; those documents were not located.

claims_per_author.author: Erwin Blumenthal
claims_per_author.work: Report on Zaire for the IMF, leaked 1982 (as reported by the Christian Science Monitor)
claims_per_author.claim: Blumenthal says corruption by Mobutu's ruling group made repayment impossible; his report put Mobutu's personal wealth at $4-5 billion, according to the Christian Science Monitor.
claims_per_author.status: The report itself was not found online; it is known from press accounts in 1982 and 1983.

claims_per_author.author: Michael Kremer (as cited by Upside Down World)
claims_per_author.work: Cited in 'IDB Debt Cancellation for Haiti', 2006
claims_per_author.claim: Kremer reports that Jean-Claude Duvalier stole $900 million.
claims_per_author.status: Toussaint and Perchellet (2010) cite a similar $900 million figure for the family's bank holdings; no court finding or official audit of the sum was found.

claims_per_author.author: Eduardo C. Tadem
claims_per_author.claim: Tadem says Philippine external debt rose from $600 million in 1965 to $26 billion in 1986.
claims_per_author.status: The Library of Congress country study confirms a rise from $2.3 billion (1970) to over $17.2 billion (1980) but gives no 1986 total; Tadem gives no source for his figures.

uncertain: 'Odious debt' is not an established rule of international law; the CRS report on Iraq says so, and creditors cut Iraq's debt through the normal Paris Club process tied to IMF conditions, not by accepting that the debt was odious.
Norway's 2006 statement does not use the words 'odious' or 'illegitimate'; it speaks of a development policy failure and shared responsibility.
Westinghouse said it paid Disini only $17 million and called it a legitimate sales commission; a New Jersey jury acquitted Westinghouse and Burns and Roe of bribery in 1993.
Ecuador's default was a suspension based on its own audit; creditors and rating agencies treated it as a default, and no court has ruled the bonds illegitimate.
The Olmos ruling found illegal acts but the crimes were time-barred, so it led to no conviction and no change to Argentina's repayment of the debt.

South Africa's 'apartheid debt' figure of R86.7 billion comes from Jubilee 2000 and includes liabilities not usually counted as sovereign debt; the finance ministry said only R240 million in foreign apartheid-era debt was outstanding in 1999.
Haiti figures on the Duvalier share of debt and the stolen sum come from campaign groups (CADTM, Foreign Policy In Focus) and a figure attributed to Michael Kremer; no official audit was checked.
Ndikumana and Boyce's capital flight estimates are calculated as residuals from balance-of-payments data and show association between borrowing and flight, not that each loan was stolen.
The Argentine debt figures of $7.5 billion (1976) and $43.5 billion (1983) come from a Jubilee 2000 account and were not checked against central bank data.
The 62-cent figure is an upper bound from a regression; the same paper's conclusion gives as much as 60 cents leaving in the same year.
check_note: Norway's 2006 step was corrected from a cancellation to an announced cancellation planned for 2007. The Argentine debt totals are now credited to Jubilee 2000, the Olmos ruling's IMF finding was reworded to what the judge wrote, and the referral to Congress is explained by the crimes being time-barred. The capital flight line from Mobutu to Swiss banks was removed because no source names Switzerland. Tadem's debt figures were taken out of the Philippines note, and the 62-cent figure was reworded as an upper bound. The unsupported statement about Austrian MPs was deleted from the Blumenthal claim. South Africa's note now says most 1999 debt service went to domestic creditors.
